title: Why do we have seasons?
question: Why do we have seasons?
audience: Curious viewers from about twelve up, anywhere in the world. They know the Earth goes round the Sun once a year; many believe summer is when the Earth is nearer the Sun.
promise: Seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis, not from its distance to the Sun: the half of the Earth leaning toward the Sun gets steeper, more concentrated sunlight and longer days, and that is its summer.

look.mood: A dark graphite stage. Amber is sunlight and summer, cool blue is winter, and they keep those meanings all film. The stage's light sits where the Sun is: left of the January Earth, right of the June Earth, high for the steep beam, low and blue for the December one. The Earth is the real globe from NASA's maps; the diagrams are thin glowing lines; panels are glass, headings are metal.

music.note: A calm pulse with no lead melody, kept low under the voice. Shot lengths are whole beats, each long enough for its recorded line, so every cut is on the grid.

facts.claim: The Earth's axis is tilted 23.44 degrees from the upright of its orbit (its obliquity); the film says and shows 23.4.
facts.source: NASA Goddard, Earth Fact Sheet (obliquity to orbit 23.44 deg); IAU value 23.4393 deg for epoch J2000

facts.claim: The Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion, 147.1 million km) in early January, about 3 January, and farthest (aphelion, 152.1 million km) in early July, about 4 July. The difference is 5.0 million km: 5.0 / 152.1 = 3.3%.
facts.source: NASA Goddard, Earth Fact Sheet (perihelion 147.095, aphelion 152.100 million km); NASA Science, Milankovitch (Orbital) Cycles (perihelion on or about 3 January, aphelion about 4 July)

facts.claim: The Earth's orbit is nearly a circle: its eccentricity is 0.0167, so the Sun sits 1.67% of the orbit's half-width off its centre. The film's orbit is a circle seen at an angle, with the Sun offset by that amount; (1 - 0.0167) / (1 + 0.0167) = 0.967 = 147.1 / 152.1.
facts.source: NASA Goddard, Earth Fact Sheet (orbit eccentricity 0.0167)

facts.claim: The axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space all year (toward Polaris), so the northern half leans toward the Sun around the June solstice (20-21 June) and away from it around the December solstice (21-22 December). The slow 26,000-year drift of the axis is left out.
facts.source: NASA Space Place, What Causes the Seasons?; NOAA SciJinks, What Causes the Seasons?

facts.claim: Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres: June to August is summer in the north and winter in the south, December to February the reverse. In early January the north is in winter.
facts.source: NASA Space Place, What Causes the Seasons?; NOAA National Weather Service, The Seasons, the Equinox and the Solstices

facts.claim: At 40 degrees north the noon Sun stands 90 - 40 + 23.44 = 73.44 degrees above the horizon at the June solstice and 90 - 40 - 23.44 = 26.56 degrees at the December solstice.
facts.source: Arithmetic from f1 (noon height = 90 - latitude + the Sun's declination); NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Solar Calculator

facts.claim: A beam of sunlight of a given width covers ground in proportion to 1 / sin(the Sun's height): 1 / sin 73.44 = 1.043 widths in June, 1 / sin 26.56 = 2.236 widths in December, so 2.236 / 1.043 = 2.14 times the ground (said as 'twice', shown as 2.1x). The light on each square metre falls in the same ratio. This is at noon at 40 N, ignoring the extra air the low beam crosses.
facts.source: Lambert's cosine law; arithmetic from f6; NASA Earth Observatory, Climate and Earth's Energy Budget (sunlight at a low angle is spread over more surface)

facts.claim: At 40 degrees north the longest day has 15 h 02 min of daylight and the shortest 9 h 20 min (said as 'fifteen hours against nine'). The drawn paths use the Sun's height = asin(sin 40 sin d + cos 40 cos d cos(15 (t - 12))) with d = +23.44 and -23.44 degrees.
facts.source: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications: Comparative Lengths of Days and Nights (40 N: 15h02m, 9h20m)

acts.title: Question
acts.goal: Ask the question in the viewer's own words, over the Earth and its leaning axis.

acts.title: Distance?
acts.goal: Meet the common guess head on: the Earth is closest to the Sun in the northern winter, so distance is not the cause.

acts.title: The tilt
acts.goal: Show what the tilt is, measure it, and show that the axis keeps its direction all year.

acts.title: Sunlight
acts.goal: The mechanism: leaning toward the Sun means steep, concentrated light and long days; leaning away means low, spread light and short days.

acts.title: Recap
acts.goal: The three ideas in one frame, then the line to remember.

shots.teaches: Asks the question the whole film answers, over the object the answer is about.
shots.screen: The real Earth (NASA maps) fills the right of the frame, centre (1420, 510), 600 px across, lit from the left, a thin amber axis through its poles leaning 23.4 degrees to the right. On the left the title in metal type, two lines, 'Why do we / have seasons?', with 'seasons?' in amber. An amber glow sits behind the title.
shots.motion: The Earth turns slowly about its leaning axis from frame 0. The title arrives letter by letter in the first 0.7 s and a sheen crosses it; the stage glow swells. At the end the title lifts away as the camera starts back.
shots.carries: The Earth and its axis, which shrink onto the orbit.
shots.transition: No cut: the title leaves upward and the camera pulls back from the Earth.
shots.sound: Music from its first beat, low. A soft shimmer as light crosses the title.
shots.check: The question is readable by 0.8 s; frame 0 already shows the lit Earth and its axis; the title does not touch the globe.

frames.note: Frame 0 is a finished picture: the Earth on the right, lit from the left, its axis drawn through it and leaning.
The question is on screen within the first second and the Earth keeps turning about its leaning axis.

shots.voice: Is summer when we're closer to the Sun?
shots.caption: Is summer when we're *closer* to the Sun?
shots.teaches: States the common guess as a guess: seasons as a matter of distance.
shots.screen: The orbit seen from above and to one side: an ellipse 1280 px wide centred (960, 455), the Sun glowing at its middle, the Earth (150 px) on the right of the orbit with its axis. A dashed amber line joins Sun and Earth; a chip under it reads 'closer = summer?'. Top right, small: 'the orbit is almost a circle, seen at an angle · sizes not to scale'. The chapter rail appears top left.
shots.motion: The Earth shrinks from the hero shot onto the orbit while the ellipse draws itself around the Sun. The Earth keeps travelling along the orbit; the dashed line follows it and the chip lands with a pop.
shots.carries: The orbit, the Sun, the Earth and the Sun-to-Earth line.
shots.transition: No cut: the dashed line turns solid as the Earth stops.
shots.sound: A soft whoosh for the pull back; a small pop when the chip lands.
shots.check: The orbit is a closed, even ellipse; the guess carries its question mark; the Earth's axis leans the same way as in the first shot.

frames.note: The camera pulls back: the Earth shrinks onto its orbit, the Sun arrives in the middle.
The guess is drawn as a guess: a dashed line from Sun to Earth, labelled as the distance, with a question mark.

draw.text: almost a circle, seen at an angle · not to scale

frames.note: The Earth has travelled on along its orbit; the dashed distance line follows it.

draw.text: almost a circle, seen at an angle · not to scale

shots.voice: No. We're closest in early January,
shots.caption: No. We're closest in *early January*,
shots.teaches: The fact that breaks the guess: the Earth is nearest the Sun in early January.
shots.screen: Same orbit. The Earth sits at the closest point (13 degrees past the December position). A solid amber line from the Sun carries '147.1 million km' and a chip 'closest · early January'. Opposite, a ghost Earth on a dashed blue line carries '152.1 million km' and 'farthest · early July'. The Sun is drawn off the middle by the orbit's real eccentricity (1.67%), so the two lines are in the ratio of the two numbers.
shots.motion: The Earth eases to a stop; the line draws solid from the Sun; the near distance appears at its value, then the far side's ghost, line and number. Nothing counts up.
shots.carries: The January Earth, which the camera goes to.
shots.transition: The camera pushes in on the January Earth; the orbit and labels fall away.
shots.sound: A tick as each distance locks.
shots.check: 147.1 sits on the January side and 152.1 on the July side; the drawn lengths differ by about 3%, not more; labels do not overlap the orbit's markers.

frames.note: The Earth stops at its closest point; the dashed line turns solid and takes its value.

draw.text: almost a circle, seen at an angle · not to scale

frames.note: Its label says when: early January. Across the orbit a ghost Earth marks the farthest point, in early July.

draw.text: almost a circle, seen at an angle · not to scale

frames.note: Both distances are read at their values; the camera starts toward the January Earth.

shots.caption: in the *northern winter*.
shots.teaches: Closest to the Sun, and yet it is winter in the north: distance cannot be the cause.
shots.screen: The January Earth from the side, centre (1180, 450), 580 px across. Sunlight comes from the left as parallel rays; the axis leans to the right, away from the Sun, and the Arctic is in the dark. Chips: 'early January' top left; 'north: winter', in cool blue, beside the northern half. The stage turns cool blue.
shots.motion: A fast push in: the Earth grows from its place on the orbit to fill the right of the frame while the rays streak in from the left. The chip lands; the globe keeps turning.
shots.carries: The Earth, which stays behind the type and returns in s06.
shots.transition: A flash on the cut; the Earth dims behind the incoming type.
shots.sound: A whoosh for the push in; a small pop for the chip.
shots.check: The lit side faces left; the axis leans right; the north polar cap is on the dark side; 'north: winter' points at the northern half.

frames.note: The January Earth fills the right of the frame, seen from the side: sunlight comes from the left, the axis leans away from it.
The north, tipped away from the Sun, is labelled: winter. The top of the globe sits in the dark.

shots.voice: The real cause is the tilt.
shots.teaches: Names the answer, in type: not the distance, the tilt.
shots.screen: Two lines of metal type, centred: 'The real cause' and 'is the tilt.' The word 'tilt.' is amber and is itself set leaning 23.4 degrees. Behind, the stage's floor and a warm amber light; no other element.
shots.motion: A flash and a shock ring on the cut. The lines slam in one after the other (scale from 1.5, blur to sharp); the accent word swings from upright to its 23.4 degree lean; a sheen crosses.
shots.carries: The lean of the word, which becomes the lean of the axis.
shots.transition: The type lifts away fast; the Earth is already arriving behind it.
shots.sound: The film's first big hit on the cut, the music ducking under it.
shots.check: Both lines are readable for over a second; the leaning word does not collide with the line above; nothing else competes.

frames.note: A flash, and the first line slams in over the dimmed stage.
The second line lands; its accent word is itself tilted by 23.4 degrees.

draw.text:
The real cause
is the tilt.

shots.voice: Earth's axis leans twenty-three point four degrees,
shots.caption: Earth's axis leans *23.4 degrees*,
shots.teaches: What the tilt is: the angle between the Earth's axis and the upright of its orbit, 23.4 degrees.
shots.screen: The Earth exactly from the side, centre (700, 470), 540 px across, its equator ringed. A level line through it is the orbit's plane (chip on the left: 'orbit's plane'); a dashed white upright stands through the centre; the amber axis leans from it. An amber arc between upright and axis, 335 px from the centre. On the right the number '23.4°' in large amber numerals, under it 'the tilt of Earth's axis'.
shots.motion: The Earth arrives large and upright. The axis, and the globe with it, swings out from the upright to exactly 23.44 degrees and the arc opens with it; then the number appears at its value and holds. The globe keeps spinning about the leaning axis.
shots.carries: The Earth with its axis, back onto the orbit.
shots.transition: The camera pulls back: the Earth shrinks to its December place on the orbit.
shots.sound: A tick as the number locks beside the arc.
shots.check: The angle drawn between the dashed upright and the axis measures 23.4 degrees; the number never shows another value; the equator ring is at right angles to the axis.

frames.note: The Earth, large on the left, seen exactly from the side. A dashed upright stands through its centre; the orbit's plane runs level.
The axis swings out from the upright to its true lean and the arc between them opens.
The number stands at its value beside the arc, and the globe keeps spinning about the leaning axis.

draw.cut: camera pulls back to the orbit

shots.voice: and points the same way all year.
shots.caption: and points the *same way* all year.
shots.teaches: The axis keeps its direction in space as the Earth goes round the Sun.
shots.screen: The orbit view again. The Earth travels from December (right) past March (far side) to June (left). At December, March, June and September a small marker stays: a disc with an amber axis line. All four axis lines are parallel. Chips name the four months; under the Sun, amber words: 'same direction, all year'. The same note as in s02 sits top right.
shots.motion: The Earth runs at a steady rate from late February to June, anticlockwise; the December marker is already behind it, March's pops as it passes, September's is drawn ahead. The axis lines never turn and glow once together.
shots.carries: The orbit with its four markers; the Earth at June.
shots.transition: The camera pushes in on the June Earth.
shots.sound: A soft whoosh for the pull back; a small tick as each marker is left.
shots.check: The four axis lines are exactly parallel; June is on the left of the Sun and December on the right; the Earth's own axis matches the markers at every moment.

frames.note: Back on the orbit. The Earth leaves December and its axis mark stays behind.
March is passed; every mark the Earth leaves leans the same way.
Four marks, four parallel axes; the Earth arrives at June, on the left of the Sun.

draw.cut: push in to the June Earth

shots.voice: In June, the north leans toward the Sun.
shots.caption: In June, the north leans *toward* the Sun.
shots.teaches: In June the same axis points the northern half toward the Sun.
shots.screen: The June Earth from the side, centre (760, 450), 580 px across. The Sun is now on the right: amber rays come in from the right edge. The axis leans right, toward them; the Arctic is in the light. Chips: 'June' top left, 'north: summer' in amber upper right, 'south: winter' in blue lower right. The 40th parallel is ringed in amber; a dot on the sunlit limb marks noon at 40° N, with its chip, and six fine rays, one beam, arrive at it.
shots.motion: A push in from the orbit. The rays arrive from the right; the hemisphere chips land in turn; the 40 degree ring, the noon dot and the six-ray beam appear. Then the dive: the camera closes on the dot and rolls by 73.4 degrees, until the ground there is level and the same six rays come down steeply.
shots.carries: The noon dot at 40° N, which becomes the ground of the next shot.
shots.transition: A dive and a roll into the dot; the ground diagram fades up exactly over the six rays where they land.
shots.sound: A whoosh for the push in; two small pops for the chips.
shots.check: The lit side faces right; the axis is the same line as in s06; the dot sits on the 40th parallel on the lit side; the north polar cap is lit.

frames.note: The June Earth, from the side. Now the Sun is on the right, and the same leaning axis points toward it.
Both halves are named: summer in the north, winter in the south.
A dot marks noon at 40 degrees north, on the sunlit side; the camera starts to dive toward it.

draw.cut: dive to the ground at 40° N

shots.voice: Steep sunlight is packed into a small patch.
shots.caption: Steep sunlight is *packed* into a small patch.
shots.teaches: The mechanism: a beam arriving steeply lands on a small patch of ground, so the patch is bright.
shots.screen: The ground at 40° N as a level slab (top at y = 740) marked in tiles. One beam of six parallel amber rays, 250 px across, comes down from the upper right at 73.4 degrees and lights a patch 261 px wide: one tile, bright. An arc at the ground reads '73°'. A measure across the beam reads 'one beam'; one under the patch reads '1×'. Left, a glass panel: 'Noon at 40° N · June', 'Sun's height 73°', 'Ground one beam lights 1×', and a gauge, 'Light on each m²', full.
shots.motion: The six rays are the ones the dive arrived on, already landing; light flows down them. The patch lights, the tiles tick in, the arc and the measure across the beam draw, the panel's rows arrive one by one and its gauge fills. A slow push.
shots.carries: The ground, the beam and the panel: the same picture returns in s11 with one thing changed.
shots.transition: A vertical whip down to the orbit.
shots.sound: A soft shimmer as the beam lands; a tick for the reading.
shots.check: The patch is exactly as wide as the beam's width divided by sin 73.4 degrees; the six rays are evenly spaced and parallel; the arc's angle is 73 degrees.

frames.note: The dive ends on the ground at 40 degrees north, at noon in June: the camera has rolled until the ground is level, the globe fades under it, and the six rays it followed come down 73 degrees above the horizon.
The whole beam has landed: six rays, a small bright patch of ground under them.
The patch is measured: one tile of ground for this beam. The panel holds the two readings.

shots.voice: In December, the north leans away.
shots.caption: In December, the north leans *away*.
shots.teaches: Half a year later the axis has not turned, so the north now leans away from the Sun.
shots.screen: The orbit view with its four markers. The Earth runs from June (left) along the near side, past September, to December (right). At December a blue chip: 'north: winter'. The month chips for June and December stay.
shots.motion: The Earth sweeps half the orbit in about a second and a half, its axis never turning; it lands at December with a small push in and the chip pops.
shots.carries: The December Earth's lean, which sets the low Sun of the next shot.
shots.transition: A horizontal whip back to the ground at 40° N.
shots.sound: A whoosh on the whip in; a pop for the chip.
shots.check: The Earth's axis stays parallel to the markers through the whole sweep; at December the top of the axis points away from the Sun.

frames.note: The orbit again: the Earth leaves June and runs the near side, past September.
It reaches December. The axis has not turned, so the north now leans away from the Sun.

shots.voice: The same beam, now low, covers twice the ground.
shots.caption: The same beam, now low, covers *twice* the ground.
shots.teaches: The same beam arriving low is spread over about twice the ground, so each part of it gets less.
shots.screen: The same slab, the same beam of six rays, now in cool blue-white and arriving at 26.6 degrees: it enters from the right edge and its patch is 559 px wide, 2.1 tiles, visibly dimmer. The June beam stays as a dashed amber ghost with its one-tile patch outlined. The arc reads '27°'; the measure across the beam now reads 'the same beam'; under the ground, '1×' and '2.1×'. The panel now reads 'December', 'Sun's height 27°', 'Ground one beam lights 2.1×', and its gauge has fallen to 47% (261 / 559).
shots.motion: The beam swings down about the patch's left end from 73.4 to 26.6 degrees; the patch stretches with it, always the beam's width divided by the sine of its height, and dims in the same proportion; the gauge falls with it. The angle's label hides during the swing and the readings swap on one frame as it lands.
shots.carries: The ground line, which becomes the horizon of the chart.
shots.transition: No cut: the beams fade, the ground stays and the sky above it becomes a chart.
shots.sound: A low whoosh as the beam swings; a tick as the reading changes.
shots.check: The December patch is 2.14 times the June one (559 px against 261 px); six rays land evenly across it; the ghost beam is still at 73 degrees.

frames.note: The same ground, the same beam. The June beam stays as a dashed ghost while the beam swings down.
At 27 degrees the six rays land far apart: the patch has stretched along the ground.
Measured against the June tile: 2.1 times the ground for the same light, so each part gets less.

draw.cut: no cut: the ground becomes the horizon

shots.voice: Days are longer too: fifteen hours against nine.
shots.caption: Days are longer too: *15 hours* against *9*.
shots.teaches: The summer Sun is also up for longer: about 15 hours of daylight against about 9 at 40° N.
shots.screen: A chart on the same ground line: the time of day runs left to right (6:00, noon, 18:00 marked under the horizon), the Sun's height runs up. Two paths computed for 40° N: June's, amber, high and wide (peak 73 degrees), and December's, blue, low and narrow (peak 27 degrees). A small Sun rides each. Chips at the peaks: 'June · 15 h of daylight', 'December · 9 h 20 min'. Under the horizon an amber bar and a blue bar span each day, from sunrise to sunset. Top right: 'the Sun's path · 40° N'.
shots.motion: The beams fade and the ground stays. The June Sun rises, draws its path and sets; December's follows, lower. Each bar grows under the horizon with its Sun, to the length of that day, and the chips land at their values.
shots.carries: The amber and blue paths, which shrink into the third recap card.
shots.transition: The chart fades as three cards rise over it.
shots.sound: A soft shimmer as the June path completes; a tick for each chip.
shots.check: The June bar is 15.0/24 of the day's width and the December bar 9.3/24; both paths peak at noon; June peaks at 73 degrees and December at 27 on the same scale.

frames.note: The ground stays as the horizon and a clock runs along it. The June Sun rises on the left.
The June path is whole: high and long. The December path starts lower and later.
Both days are measured along the horizon: about 15 hours of daylight against about 9.

draw.cut: the chart folds into a card

shots.voice: Steep light and long days: that's summer.
shots.caption: *Steep light* and *long days*: that's summer.
shots.teaches: The whole answer in one frame: the tilt, the steep light, the long day.
shots.screen: Three glass cards in a row, each 520 x 420: 'The axis leans 23.4°' with a small Earth and its axis; 'Steep light, small patch' with the steep amber beam beside the low blue one on their two patches; 'Long days: 15 h against 9' with the two Sun paths and their day bars. Above them: 'What makes a summer'.
shots.motion: The cards rise in turn with a slight forward tilt and settle; they breathe; at the end they shrink together toward the centre.
shots.carries: The amber of the three cards, which gathers into the flash.
shots.transition: The cards collapse to the centre and a flash opens the last frame.
shots.sound: Three soft card sounds as they land.
shots.check: Each small picture agrees with its big one: the axis at 23.4 degrees, the patches about 1 to 2.1, the June path higher and wider than December's.

frames.note: Three cards rise, one after another, each with the small picture of its idea.
All three are up: the tilt, the steep light on a small patch, the long day.
The cards hold, breathing, then gather toward the centre for the last line.

shots.voice: It's the tilt, not the distance.
shots.screen: The Earth, 380 px across, at the top centre (960, 300), leaning on its amber axis and turning. Under it, two lines of metal type: 'It's the tilt,' with 'tilt' in amber, and 'not the distance.' Under them a small line in mono capitals: 'EARTH'S AXIS · 23.4°'. A warm light on the floor below.
shots.motion: A flash; the Earth settles from large to its place; the two lines arrive by letter; a sheen crosses; then the frame holds for over two seconds, the light swelling and a 2% push in.
shots.transition: The film ends on this frame; the music fades under it.
shots.sound: The second big hit on the cut; the music fades out over the hold.
shots.check: The line is fully readable at least two seconds before the end; the axis leans 23.4 degrees; nothing moves abruptly in the hold.

frames.note: A flash; the Earth settles at the top of the frame, leaning, still turning.
The line to remember arrives by letter under it.

draw.text:
It's the tilt,
not the distance.

frames.note: The poster holds for more than two seconds, breathing: the light swells and the frame pushes in a little.

draw.text:
It's the tilt,
not the distance.
